name: Adonis
description: Sherry and sweet vermouth with orange bitters — a low-proof aperitif named after a Broadway musical that ran for over 500 nights in 1884.
funFact: Adonis was the first musical in Broadway history to run more than 500 performances, and the Waldorf's bartender named the drink to catch its publicity.

steps: Combine everything in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20 seconds — this is low-proof, so watch the dilution.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the top.

name: Chrysanthemum
description: Dry vermouth, Bénédictine and a whisper of absinthe. No base spirit at all, and far more interesting than that sounds.
funFact: It appears in Hugo Ensslin's 1916 'Recipes for Mixed Drinks', one of the last American cocktail books published before Prohibition shut the genre down.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the surface and discard.

name: Diplomat
description: Two vermouths and a spoon of maraschino. A vermouth cocktail from the era when ordering one was completely unremarkable.
funFact: Before Prohibition, vermouth-only cocktails were standard afternoon drinking in American hotels — the category vanished so completely that it had to be rediscovered a century later.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 20 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry and a lemon twist.
Serve as an aperitif before dinner.

name: Coronation
description: Sherry, dry vermouth and maraschino — created for the coronation of Edward VII and served at the Knickerbocker.
funFact: Edward VII's 1902 coronation was postponed at two days' notice for an emergency appendectomy, but the cocktails named for it went ahead regardless.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 20 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface.
Serve well chilled.

name: Turf Cocktail
description: Gin and dry vermouth with maraschino and absinthe — a Martinez cousin from the racetrack era, drier and sharper than the Tuxedo.
funFact: The Turf, the Tuxedo and the Martinez are essentially the same drink with the dial turned differently, and nineteenth-century bar books rarely agreed on which was which.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an olive or a lemon twist.
Serve very cold.

name: Income Tax
description: A Bronx with bitters added — gin, both vermouths and orange juice, named for the tax that arrived in 1913 and never left.
funFact: The American federal income tax became permanent in 1913, and the cocktail named after it appeared almost immediately — bartenders have always found a drink in bad news.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.
Serve immediately.

name: Bobby Burns
description: A Rob Roy with Bénédictine in place of the bitters — honeyed herbs against Scotch, named for the poet with an extra B.
funFact: Every bar book spells it differently — Bobby Burns, Bobbie Burns, Robert Burns — and the Savoy insists it is 'one of the very best whisky cocktails'.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.
Serve cold.

name: Affinity
description: A perfect Rob Roy: Scotch with both vermouths and Angostura, balanced between sweet and dry rather than committing to either.
funFact: 'Perfect' in cocktail language never means excellent — it means split evenly between sweet and dry vermouth, a convention that confuses nearly everyone who orders one.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry.
Serve very cold.

name: Old Pal
description: A Boulevardier stripped dry: rye, dry vermouth and Campari in equal parts. Leaner, more bitter and considerably more bracing.
funFact: Harry MacElhone recorded it at his Paris bar alongside the Boulevardier, crediting it to a sports writer who called everyone 'old pal'.

steps: Stir all three over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the top.
Serve without garnish beyond the twist.

name: Scofflaw
description: Rye, dry vermouth, lemon and grenadine — named for the word Americans invented in 1924 to describe people who drank anyway.
funFact: 'Scofflaw' was the winning entry in a 1924 Boston competition to coin a word for a Prohibition lawbreaker; Harry's Bar in Paris had a cocktail named after it within weeks.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
Serve immediately.

name: Diamondback
description: Rye, applejack and yellow Chartreuse in equal measure. Described by one writer as a drink that will 'put hair on your chest' — accurately.
funFact: It comes from the Diamondback Lounge in Baltimore's Lord Baltimore Hotel, and at equal parts with no dilution from citrus it is one of the stiffest classics still in circulation.

steps: Stir all three over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
No garnish is traditional.
Serve very cold and sip slowly.

name: De La Louisiane
description: New Orleans' other great rye drink: rye, sweet vermouth, Bénédictine and absinthe, from a restaurant that served it as the house cocktail.
funFact: Restaurant de la Louisiane on Iberville Street served it as its signature; it is essentially a Vieux Carré with the cognac removed and the Bénédictine turned up.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with three brandied cherries.
Serve cold.

name: Fancy Free
description: Bourbon with maraschino standing in for sugar, and two kinds of bitters. An Old Fashioned that went to finishing school.
funFact: Maraschino here does the sweetening job that sugar does in an Old Fashioned, which is why the drink tastes richer without actually being sweeter.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain over a large cube in a rocks glass.
Express an orange twist over the surface and drop it in.
Serve immediately.

name: Improved Whiskey Cocktail
description: The Old Fashioned with maraschino and absinthe added — 'improved' was a genuine nineteenth-century menu category, not a boast.
funFact: Jerry Thomas listed 'improved' versions of several cocktails in 1876, meaning ones upgraded with maraschino and absinthe — the word described a recipe family, not an opinion.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain over a large cube in a rocks glass.
Express a lemon twist over the surface.
Serve immediately.

name: Morning Glory Fizz
description: Scotch, absinthe, lemon and egg white under soda — a Victorian hangover cure that took the previous night's absinthe as the remedy.
funFact: Victorian bar manuals recommended it explicitly as a morning restorative, on the reasoning that a little of what hurt you was the cure — advice modern medicine does not endorse.

steps: Dry-shake everything except the soda for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Strain into a chilled highball glass with no ice.
Top slowly with soda water to lift the foam.
Serve without garnish.

name: Sloe Gin Fizz
description: Sloe gin, lemon and soda over ice — pink, tart and gentle, and the reason most Americans have heard of sloe gin at all.
funFact: Sloe gin is not gin but a liqueur made by steeping blackthorn sloes in gin and sugar — traditionally picked after the first frost, which softens the fruit.

steps: Shake the sloe gin, lemon juice and syrup with ice.
Strain into a highball glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and a cherry.

name: Chicago Fizz
description: Rum and ruby port shaken with lemon and egg white. Darker and richer than a fizz has any right to be.
funFact: The fizz family once ran to dozens of named variations — silver with egg white, golden with yolk, royal with the whole egg — of which only a handful survive on menus.

steps: Dry-shake everything but the soda for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Strain into a chilled highball with no ice.
Top gently with soda water.
Serve immediately.

name: Whiskey Smash
description: Bourbon, lemon and mint pounded together over crushed ice — a julep that took a lemon along.
funFact: Jerry Thomas defined the smash in 1862 as 'a julep on a small plan', and the form barely changed in the 160 years since.

steps: Muddle the lemon quarters with the syrup in a shaker.
Add the mint and press gently — do not shred it.
Add the bourbon and ice, then shake hard for 10 seconds.
Double-strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a mint bouquet.

name: Brandy Flip
description: Brandy, a whole egg and sugar, shaken to a custardy foam and dusted with nutmeg. The oldest cocktail template still in use.
funFact: Flips originally involved plunging a red-hot iron 'flip dog' into a mug of spiked ale to make it froth — the egg version is the domesticated descendant.

steps: Dry-shake the brandy, egg and syrup without ice for 20 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a small chilled wine glass.
Grate fresh nutmeg generously over the top.

name: Coffee Cocktail
description: Port, cognac and a whole egg. Contains no coffee at all — it was named for looking like one.
funFact: Jerry Thomas named it for its appearance rather than its contents, and then had to explain in print that it contained no coffee whatsoever.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 20 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for 15 seconds more.
Double-strain into a small wine glass.
Grate nutmeg over the surface.

name: Bourbon Milk Punch
description: Bourbon, milk, sugar and vanilla over ice with nutmeg. New Orleans brunch, and a genuine hangover institution.
funFact: Along with the Ramos Gin Fizz and the Sazerac, it is one of the three drinks New Orleans considers acceptable before noon.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds until frothy.
Strain into a rocks glass over fresh ice.
Grate nutmeg generously over the top.

name: Presbyterian
description: Whiskey with ginger ale and soda in equal measure — the highball for people who find straight ginger ale too sweet.
funFact: The split of ginger ale and soda is the whole idea: the ginger carries flavour while the soda cuts the sugar, which is why the drink outlived the whiskey-and-ginger.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the whiskey.
Top with equal parts ginger ale and soda water.
Stir once and garnish with a lemon twist.

name: Mamie Taylor
description: Scotch, lime and ginger beer — the 1899 hit that the Moscow Mule copied wholesale fifty years later with vodka.
funFact: Named for a Broadway singer, it was a national craze in 1900; the Moscow Mule is structurally the same drink and got all the credit.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the Scotch and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Nevada
description: Rum with grapefruit and lime over sugar and bitters — a Cuban-era sour that deserved better than obscurity.
funFact: It appears in Havana bar books of the 1930s alongside the Daiquiri and Mary Pickford, part of a whole grapefruit-and-rum family that never travelled.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a grapefruit twist.
Serve immediately.

name: Hotel Nacional
description: Rum, apricot, pineapple and lime from Havana's grandest hotel — tropical without tipping into a tiki drink.
funFact: The Hotel Nacional opened in 1930 and hosted everyone from Churchill to the mafia summit that inspired The Godfather Part II; its bar produced this alongside the Mary Pickford.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a thin apricot or pineapple slice.
Serve cold.

name: Air Mail
description: Rum, honey and lime topped with champagne — a Daiquiri that took flight, named for the airmail service of the 1930s.
funFact: It appears in a 1949 Bacardi promotional booklet, though the name dates it to the era when airmail stamps were exotic enough to name a drink after.

steps: Shake the rum, honey syrup and lime juice hard with ice.
Strain into a chilled flute or coupe.
Top slowly with champagne.
Garnish with a mint sprig.

name: Gibson
description: A Martini garnished with a pickled onion instead of an olive. That single swap changes the whole drink, which is the point.
funFact: The onion is not decoration — its vinegar and sweetness measurably change the finish, which is why Gibson drinkers are so specific about it.

steps: Stir the gin and vermouth over ice for 30 seconds.
Strain into a thoroughly chilled coupe.
Drop in two cocktail onions on a pick.
Serve immediately, very cold.

name: Dirty Martini
description: A Martini with olive brine stirred in. Divisive by design, and the most-ordered Martini variation in America.
funFact: Franklin Roosevelt is often credited with popularising it — he mixed Martinis at the White House and was reportedly heavy-handed with the olive juice.

steps: Stir the gin, vermouth and olive brine over ice for 30 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with three olives on a pick.
Serve very cold.

name: Black Manhattan
description: A Manhattan with amaro in place of the sweet vermouth — darker, more bitter and noticeably more serious.
funFact: Todd Smith created it at Bourbon & Branch in San Francisco around 2005, and it did more than any other drink to put Averna on American back bars.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a brandied cherry.
Serve cold.

name: Bensonhurst
description: Rye, dry vermouth, maraschino and Cynar — the driest of the Brooklyn neighbourhood series and the most bitter.
funFact: Chad Solomon created it at Milk & Honey as part of the Brooklyn-variation family that also produced the Red Hook and the Greenpoint.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
No garnish is traditional.
Serve very cold.

name: Rosita
description: A tequila Negroni with both vermouths — reposado against Campari, from Gary Regan's 1991 bartender's bible.
funFact: Gary Regan printed it in 'The Bartender's Bible' in 1991, years before anyone else was seriously mixing tequila into stirred aperitif drinks.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
Express a lemon twist over the top and drop it in.
Serve cold.

name: Kingston Negroni
description: A Negroni built on Jamaican overproof rum. The funk of the rum against Campari's bitterness is the whole argument, and it works.
funFact: Joaquín Simó created it at Death & Co, using Smith & Cross — a high-ester Jamaican rum whose banana-and-overripe-fruit character survives even Campari.

steps: Stir all three over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain over a large cube in a rocks glass.
Express an orange twist over the surface and drop it in.
Serve immediately.

name: Mezcal Negroni
description: Smoke where the juniper was. Mezcal turns the Negroni savoury and campfire-scented without touching its structure.
funFact: The Negroni's equal-parts structure is unusually robust — swapping the gin for mezcal, rum, whiskey or sherry all produce drinks that still work, which is why the variations are endless.

steps: Stir all three over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain over a large cube in a rocks glass.
Express an orange twist over the top and drop it in.
Serve immediately.
